connections.feedback: Yes! California's coast faces west, and the Pacific Ocean is the big ocean on the western side of the country.
The Indian Ocean is on the other side of the world, near Asia and Africa. California's ocean is the one to the west of North America.
Not quite. The Atlantic Ocean is on the eastern side of the country. California is on the opposite side, in the west.
The Arctic Ocean is far to the north, near the top of the world. It does not touch California. Try the ocean on the western side.

The Indian Ocean does not touch the United States mainland. The ocean on the eastern coast has a different name.
The Pacific Ocean is on the western side of the country. Georgia and Florida are in the east, so think of the other big ocean.

Tacoma is a port city not far from the capital. It is a common mix-up, but the capital is Olympia.

The Census West region has the Rocky Mountain and Pacific states. Texas is not in that group, even though it is in the western half of the country.

connections.feedback: That adds only one hour, which would be the gap between neighboring zones. Pacific and Eastern are three zones apart.
That subtracts three hours. Going east, the clock is later, not earlier. Add three hours to a Pacific time to get Eastern.

Correct. Eastern time is three hours ahead of Pacific time, so 3:00 p.m. Pacific is 6:00 p.m. Eastern.

sets.label: Why the east side of the Cascades is dry (Grades 9-12, intermediate)

origin.author: READY builder
origin.source_reference: Original draft material; not an official assessment; awaiting owner review

connections.feedback: Correct. Air rising over a mountain cools and drops moisture on the side facing the wind. The far side, the rain shadow, gets much less.
Rivers do not remove rain from the sky. The difference comes from air moving over the mountains and losing its moisture.
The reverse is true. The western side is closer to the Pacific Ocean, which is why it gets the moist air first.
Soil color does not stop rain from falling. Rainfall differs because of how the mountains force moist air to rise and cool.

sets.label: Why the east side of the Cascades is dry (General adult, intermediate)

origin.author: READY builder
origin.source_reference: Original draft material; not an official assessment; awaiting owner review

connections.feedback: Rock does not soak rain out of the sky. The dryness comes from air cooling and losing moisture as it climbs the mountains.
Correct. This is called a rain shadow. Rising air cools and sheds moisture, so the downwind side is left dry.
Ocean currents affect coastal climate, but they do not explain the sharp dry line east of the Cascades. Mountains forcing air upward do.
Winds often are weaker inland, but the main cause is moisture lost over the mountains, not a lack of wind. This is a partial idea, not the best explanation.
connections.notes: Partly true that inland air patterns change, but it is not the main mechanism. Marked ambiguous so the feedback can redirect.

connections.feedback: Yes. Cities grow and change over time. The capital stayed where it was chosen, while others later grew larger.
Yes. Picking a smaller city could avoid giving one big rival an advantage, which is a common reason.
Yes. In many states, leaders wanted a capital near the middle, so people from all parts could reach it.
No. No such rule exists. Capitals vary in size, and some are among their state's largest cities.
